note: Extracted from docs/DECISIONS.md 1.3-1.4 and docs/ATLAS.md 11. Pre-training decides what the model knows; post-training decides how it behaves. IMPORTANT: every count below is a PROPOSED BUDGET, not a measurement and not a figure read off any published model. docs/DECISIONS.md states them with a tilde and cites nothing. They are recorded here as estimates and the `reference` block gives the published numbers they should be judged against.

stages.name: Supervised fine-tuning
stages.plain: Show it worked examples of the job you want done
stages.why: The model has read the internet but has never been shown what a good answer looks like. SFT is the demonstration set.

splits.name: agentic
splits.why: Multi-step tool use is the capability least present in raw web text.

splits.name: code
splits.why: Matches the agentic budget, because agentic work here is mostly code work.

splits.name: Indic conversation
splits.why: IndicTalk, UPDESH, IndicAlign-Instruct. The only tier that teaches how these languages are actually spoken.

splits.name: reasoning
splits.why: Long chains, shown rather than described.

splits.name: India-context factuality
splits.why: Answers that assume Indian law, geography and institutions as default.

splits.name: safety
splits.why: Refusals and boundaries, taught in every language rather than translated into them.

stages.name: Preference alignment
stages.plain: Show it two answers and which one people preferred
stages.why: Demonstrations teach a good answer. Preferences teach which of two plausible answers is better — a judgement you cannot write down as a rule.

splits.name: India factuality and plural perspectives
splits.why: Contested questions where a single confident answer is the wrong shape.

splits.name: safety incl. transliterated slurs
splits.why: Romanised Hindi abuse passes every English filter. It has to be learned, not matched.

splits.name: code quality
splits.why: Both answers compile; one is maintainable.

splits.name: agentic tool-selection and termination
splits.why: Knowing when to stop is a preference, not a fact.

splits.name: stop discipline
splits.why: Models over-answer. This is where that gets corrected.

splits.name: Indic register
splits.why: Judged by native speakers, not translated from English judgements.

stages.name: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards
stages.plain: Let it try, and check the answer automatically
stages.why: No human grades these. A test suite or a Python interpreter says pass or fail, so the model can practise millions of times without anyone watching.

splits.name: math
splits.why: Python-verified — the answer is checkable exactly.

splits.name: code
splits.why: Unit tests are the reward function.

splits.name: Indic issue to patch
splits.why: The differentiator. See below — this dataset does not exist yet.

splits.name: verifiable instruction-following
splits.why: Constraints a checker can confirm were obeyed.

differentiator.title: Verifiable reward in Hindi, at zero annotation cost
differentiator.how: Translate only the issue text of SWE-smith instances into Indic languages. Tests and patches stay byte-identical, so the verifier still works unchanged.
differentiator.why_it_matters: A Bengali-language GitHub issue resolving into a passing patch is the demo that proves this is not an English model with a flag set. Nothing like it exists in any catalogue.

alignment_findings.finding: Safety alignment does not transfer across languages
alignment_findings.consequence: You must red-team in all 22 languages. Extrapolating from English is how a model ships safe in English and unsafe everywhere else.
English SFT carries further than expected, which is why the SFT budget is not 22 parallel corpora.

alignment_findings.finding: Preference alignment must be natively multilingual
alignment_findings.consequence: Pairs generated in the language and judged by in-language annotators. Translated preference data teaches translated taste.

reference.note: What post-training sets other people actually built, so the proposal above can be compared rather than merely asserted. Gathered by web research in August 2026.

models.preference_note: 337K for the 8B checkpoint, 361K for the 70B. Roughly 30% of the collected prompts converted to preference data.
models.source: arXiv:2411.15124, Tulu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training (Allen Institute for AI)
models.why_here: The only fully open post-training recipe at this level of detail — mixture, sizes and method all published, including the RLVR stage this plan borrows.

models.preference_note: Not broken out. The 10M is human-annotated fine-tuning examples across the whole post-training stack.
models.source: Meta, Llama 3 model card and technical report
models.why_here: The frontier end of the range, and a reminder that the gap between an open recipe and an industrial one is an order of magnitude of human annotation.

reference.finding: This plan's 3M SFT examples sit between Tulu 3's 939K and Llama 3's 10M+, which is a defensible place for a 40B seed to be. Its preference budget is not. Tulu 3 converts preference data at roughly 36% of its SFT size; this plan proposes 200K against 3M, which is 6.7%. Either the SFT budget is three times larger than it needs to be, or the preference budget is five times smaller than published practice — and nothing in the plan says which.
